Funding acknowledgments (FAs) provide a potential but underexplored source for mapping global research funding flows. This study develops a framework for constructing global funding flow measures using FA data from Dimensions and assesses both the opportunities and limitations of this approach. We compare total and inter-regional funding flows based on funding grant information available in FAs of scientific publications. Our analysis identifies a key limitation arising from collaborative publications, where funding is attributed at the publication level rather than to individual authors. This obscures the interpretation of cross-border funding flows. We show that this attribution structure introduces systematic ambiguity and limits the validity of FA-based analyses. We argue that disaggregated, author-level funding attribution is essential for accurately tracing funding flows. This requires coordinated action among funders, publishers, and researchers, as well as the adoption of more standardized, machine-readable FAs formats.

As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into everyday information-seeking and decision-making contexts, concerns have grown regarding their tendency to produce inaccurate or fabricated outputs, such as hallucinations. This study investigates factors associated with users’ intention to verify LLM-generated information, focusing on three domains: user competencies (digital literacy, information literacy, and AI literacy), sociotechnical attitudes (trust in AI and privacy concerns), and usage characteristics (frequency of use and perceived task importance). Analysis of a survey of U.S. adult LLM users shows that AI literacy is the strongest and most consistent predictor of verification intention: individuals with higher AI literacy report greater intention to verify LLM outputs, including cross-checking information, requesting supporting evidence, and reporting inaccurate information to LLM platforms. Digital literacy shows a positive but smaller association with verification intention, while information literacy is not significantly related. In addition, higher privacy concerns and greater perceived task importance are positively associated with verification intention, although these effects are smaller in magnitude compared to AI literacy. These findings provide valuable initial evidence about user-level factors that shape information verification behaviors in human-AI interaction, addressing one of the pressing concerns in increasingly AI-mediated information environments.

Storytelling is widely used in education, but it is still most often treated as a tool for engagement, illustration, or representation rather than as a structure for thought. I theorize provocative storytelling as a pedagogical construct that positions narrative as a site of inquiry. Rather than delivering meaning, provocative stories are deliberately designed to generate interpretive tension, inviting learners into processes of questioning, perspective-taking, and dialogic reasoning. Drawing on narrative theory, dialogism, critical literacy, and inquiry-based learning, the article articulates the design principles that distinguish provocative storytelling from adjacent approaches such as case-based learning and dilemma pedagogy. It argues that contemporary pedagogical practices often privilege coherence, clarity, and transmission at the expense of interpretive engagement, limiting opportunities for students to grapple with complexity, ambiguity, and competing perspectives (Biesta, 2010). By framing narrative as an epistemic space rather than a rhetorical device, this article contributes a theoretically grounded approach to pedagogy that foregrounds meaning-making as a social, cultural, and interpretive process. The article concludes with implications for curriculum design, teacher education, and classroom practice, particularly in contexts that seek to engage learners in critical, interdisciplinary, and culturally responsive inquiry.

While most research funding is national, international funding plays a relatively important role, particularly for some regions of the Global South. However, the extent of funding flows between world regions remains unclear. This study represents a first attempt to map global research funding flows based on a set of grant metadata from Dimensions, augmented with data from the Gates Foundation and the European Commission (CORDIS). We find major regional gaps in the data outside of the leading scientific regions. With the data currently available, we find that Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa are the biggest recipients of inter-regional funding, with North America as main funder, and that over the last 25 years, total annual research funding has grown to above USD 60 billion, while inter-regional funding flows have stagnated at around USD 1.6 billion per year. These insights are contingent on data availability, raising the urgency for improving funding metadata infrastructures.

Recent studies of visual working memory (VWM) have investigated a population coding framework, in which items in memory are coded by an array of noisy, tuned detectors. Within this framework, heavy-tailed distributions of memory errors found in continuous-outcome VWM tasks reflect noise in the detector array rather than guessing. Studies have compared alternative tuning functions and detector noise distributions, finding differences in fit in some cases and substantial model mimicry in others. We used population coding models to look for evidence of a sample-size model of memory capacity, which predicts that memory strength will follow an inverse square-root law in set size, reflecting changes in the neural resources available to represent items. In two experiments, we independently manipulated the difficulty of the memory and decision tasks by varying the set size and the color saturation of the stimuli and the response wheel, respectively. We compared four population coding models and found that: (1) a von Mises tuning function provided better model fit and more stable estimates than a similarity-based, exponential-decay tuning function; (2) normal and Gumbel noise functions provided comparably good fits, but different patterns of parameter estimates; (3) Depending on task complexity, the amplitude of tuning function followed either an inverse square-root law or power law in set size, as predicted by the sample-size and attention-weighted sample-size model, respectively. Our results provided evidence for the sample-size account of VWM capacity in continuous outcome tasks and highlighted the potential of the models to be more than just measurement models.

Ideal experiments (IEs) describe hypothetical studies that we would carry out without practical, ethical, or resource-related constraints. IEs can help us to identify pitfalls and deficiencies in causal research projects (e.g., Angrist and Pischke 2008). We contend that the focus of IEs is too narrow and introduce the more general notion of ideal research designs (IRDs). IRDs go beyond IEs in that they also speak to issues such as measurement errors that are rarely the focus of IEs. After reviewing how researchers define and advocate using IEs, we discuss what components IRDs should encompass drawing on well-known error frameworks. After an applied example that explains how IRDs can be used in research, we explore how empirical researchers are using IRDs. While we find few examples, they attest to the usefulness of IRDs to evaluate research designs that have been realized or are planned for the future.

The history of autism scholarship is traditionally narrated as a sequence of progressive clinical discoveries. The argument advanced here proposes an alternative genealogical framework, tracing how the pathology paradigm reproduces itself independently of its scientific validity through mechanisms of institutional inheritance. Informed by epistemic injustice theory and the DisCrit framework, the analysis demonstrates how early bidirectional understandings of autistic traits were actively displaced by five historical nodes of clinical authority: Kanner, Bettelheim, Asperger, Lovaas, and Autism Speaks. To explain the durability of this deficit-based orientation across paradigmatic shifts, the analysis introduces a transmission model comprising three recursive structures: interpretive prefiguration, credential monopolization, and administrative sedimentation. Together, these mechanisms transitioned the Autistic community from a state of hermeneutical lacuna into a condition of hermeneutical domination. This theoretical model is subsequently applied to the contemporary United States federal health apparatus, documenting how 2025 and 2026 executive branch funding allocations, rhetorical strategies, and judicial rulings on compliance-oriented interventions function as convergent instruments of epistemic severance. Dismantling this living infrastructure ultimately requires accountable research governance that untethers federal grant eligibility from normative institutional affiliation and centers the intersectional knowledge produced by the Autistic community.


Keywords: critical autism studies, epistemic injustice, hermeneutical domination, DisCrit, federal health policy, structural ableism, Double Empathy Problem, neurodiversity

This article analyzes BPE tokenization in Polish as a test case for a broader problem: the limits of statistical segmentation in an inflectional language. The starting point is the question of whether, and to what extent, frequency-based tokenization preserves units that are relevant for the linguistic description of Polish: orthographic form, the segmentation-phonemic level, syllable structure, logotomes, prefixes, derivational bases, inflectional endings, grammatical form, and the position of the speaking subject.
The empirical material includes the tokenization of diagnostic words, a simple children’s text, selected forms from the Preamble to the Constitution of the Republic of Poland, word-family tests, and examples containing Polish diacritics and nasal vowels. The analysis shows that BPE tokenizers may locally produce segments that coincide with syllabic, logotomic, or morphologically interpretable divisions, but they remain fundamentally dependent on the frequency of written forms. They do not systematically move from orthographic representation to the segmentation-phonemic level or to context-dependent phonetic realization.
The results also indicate that BPE stabilizes not grammatical categories themselves, but frequent surface fragments of their exponents. Segments such as -y, -ich, -ni, or -ć may appear as stable tokens or parts of tokens, but this does not amount to preserving the full grammatical form. A form such as ustanawiamy is not merely a sequence ending in -y; it is a verbal form anchored in conjugation, person, number, tense, mood, and aspect.
The article develops the concept of grammatical form anchoring, arguing that in Polish a form may not only encode syntactic relations, but also establish the position of the speaking subject. In forms such as poszłam, zrobiłam, or byłam, the grammatical “I” need not be expressed by a separate pronoun, because it is anchored in inflection. In interaction with AI, this reveals an additional problem: a language model does not possess its own stable grammatical “I”, but reconstructs it contextually, often mirroring the user’s forms or shifting grammatical gender.
I propose treating Rocławski’s segmentation-flexional forms not as a description of how BPE operates, but as a diagnostic framework for assessing the quality of tokenization boundaries. The findings lead to the research hypothesis that more stable modeling of Polish may require several layers: sublexical stabilization inspired by Rocławski’s system, anchoring grammatical form in the inflectional system, representing sentence patterns and verbal valency structure, and maintaining the position of the grammatical “I” in dialogue. From this perspective, the problem of Polish AI is not reducible to reducing the number of tokens. Rather, it concerns maintaining relations between orthographic representation, word form, grammatical function, sentence position, and the position of the speaking subject.

Public engagement with climate change remains uneven despite growing exposure to climate risks and communication. While climate inaction is often explained as a result of weak concern, less attention has been given to whether inaction itself shapes how people interpret climate responsibility and information. Drawing on cognitive dissonance theory, this study examines climate inaction from a behavior-to-attitude perspective, proposing that limited action may trigger self-justifying processes that distance individuals from climate risks and shape climate-related information engagement. A nationwide online survey of 500 Malaysian adults was analysed using structural equation modelling. Results broadly supported the proposed model: climate inaction was associated with moral disengagement, greater psychological distance, lower climate concern, and higher climate skepticism, while climate information seeking played a complex role in these attitudinal outcomes. The findings suggest that climate inaction may actively sustain future disengagement by reshaping psychological and communicative responses to climate change.

Drawing on the latest interdisciplinary insights on human-technology interaction, this conceptual chapter explains key perspectives and frameworks of how people adopt, interact with, and experience technology. After introducing core ethical aspects of technology, the chapter takes a critical stance on the promises and pitfalls of disruptive technological advancement—including but not limited to AI. Combining organizational, socio-psychological, and ethical perspectives on human-technology interaction, fundamental challenges of human control over digital technologies—which are not only tools but also agents and infrastructures—are explained. Based on this literature review, the chapter highlights and explains important blind spots within the commonly used models of human-technology interaction and discusses unresolved issues of user-technology value alignment, accountability, and control.

Do moral norms influence citizens' tolerance of anti-system behavior by politicians? Although moral norms are often invoked as guardrails, their measurement and causal influence in politics remain understudied. We theorize the link between moral norms, personal judgments, and attitudinal consequences and test our theory in a pre-registered survey experiment with financial incentives. Respondents faced moral trade-offs concerning personal scandals, political violence, corruption, and anti-democratic actions. Using a second-order approach to elicit beliefs about what others consider morally wrong, we find that norms against democratic violations are descriptively weaker than norms against scandal and corruption; both lag behind norms against violence. Causal evidence shows that norms primarily shift judgments when respondents face large discrepancies from their initial perceived norm and have strong conformity motives. However, this largely does not translate into attitudinal shifts. The findings shed light on the concept of moral norms and detail their consequences and limitations for politics.

Recent contributions by danah boyd (2026) and Törnberg & Rogers (2026) have argued that social media platforms have undergone a fundamental transformation: what once enabled reciprocal social interaction has become a landscape of parasocial observation, algorithmic broadcasting, and post-social fragmentation. This essay takes these empirical diagnoses seriously while subjecting their conceptual foundations to critical scrutiny. It argues that both contributions operate with an implicitly normative and analytically underdetermined concept of sociality, one that reduces a theoretically complex category to a historically particular manifestation. Drawing on the sociology of knowledge (Berger & Luckmann), communicative constructivism (Knoblauch, Keller), actor-network theory (Latour), feminist materialism (Haraway), and the concept of object-centred sociality (Knorr Cetina), the essay argues that sociality was never independent of its material and technical mediations, and that the relationship to objects, algorithms, and non-human actors is itself a form of sociality rather than its absence. A further objection is epistemological: ‘social media’ was never a scientifically precise category but an ethnocategory, an industry term and journalistic shorthand whose normative charge has been unreflectively adopted as an analytical framework. The essay concludes that the current debate diagnoses less the end of ‘social media’ than the crisis of a never-sufficiently-defined scientific category, and calls for a more systematic engagement with theoretical resources, available both within and beyond communication research, that may help to specify what the social is, and where it resides in contemporary digital environments.

Clarity and precision are vital in science communication, yet sociology is often criticized for using overly complex language. In this study, we examine the complexity of sociological writing using an original dataset of 1,700 full-text articles from three major German journals. We validate a composite measure to investigate complexity over time and across methodological orientations, which past work has shown to follow different research conventions. We find that peak textual complexity in sociological articles increases over time and is systematically related to methodological choices. Next, we examine the relationship between complexity and citation-based impact. In contrast with findings from other disciplines, our results provide no evidence for complex writing to either harm or boost the number of citations per article. Finally, we demonstrate a simple workflow that uses our composite measure alongside generative artificial intelligence. This approach can identify highly complex passages and support targeted revision, thereby contributing to clearer communication and accessibility in academia and beyond.

Taking the global gauge constraint \(\hat{G}^a|\Psi\rangle=0\) as the first principle, this paper constructs a physical theoretical framework. The theory establishes a mathematical system centered on fusion \(\infty\)-categories, and, relying on the self-consistency closure axiom, rigorously proves the \(E_8\) skeleton theorem, thereby demonstrating at the mathematical level the objective necessity of the gauge group and matter representations. On this basis, starting from the physical mechanism whereby the symmetry breaking and local evolution of quantum-information-correlated pure states violate the global gauge constraint \(\hat{G}^a|\Psi\rangle=0\) and thereby excite an error-correcting response of the internal gauge fields, the intrinsic mechanisms and low-energy effective Lagrangians of the electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions are derived in a unified manner. At the same time, through symmetry breaking and informational local evolution, quantum-information-correlated pure states generate classical matter fields, which induce an error-correcting effect in spacetime geometry and produce spacetime curvature, from which Einstein's general relativity naturally emerges. The masses of gauge bosons originate directly from the characteristic depth of quantum information localization; the Higgs boson is viewed as the collective amplitude mode of an order parameter; unitarity is realized through nonlocal error correction in the quantum information network; and the Higgs hierarchy problem is completely eliminated. The Standard Model gauge group \(SU(3)_c\times SU(2)_L\times U(1)_Y\), three generations of fermions, as well as coupling constants, mass spectra, mixing angles, and other physical parameters, all become computable eigenvalues of the \(E_8\) representation theory within the global gauge constraint framework. It provides the origin of causality and the arrow of time, and self-consistently explains quantum entanglement nonlocality, the quantum measurement problem, and puzzles related to the observer. At the qualitative level, this theory puts forward a set of exclusive and strictly falsifiable physical predictions: no supersymmetric particles and no extra spatial dimensions; absolute stability of the proton; no graviton; the tensor-to-scalar ratio of primordial gravitational waves tends to zero; deviations in Higgs couplings at the per mille level; a dark energy equation of state that can cross \(w=-1\); and no primordial black holes or magnetic monopoles. At the present stage, this research is at the stage of a theoretical program; the entire mathematical framework has been rigorously proved, while some physical derivations only provide principled schemes, demonstrating that it is a feasible research route to generate all cosmic structures layer by layer from a minimal set of first principles.

What we learn from open-ended survey data depends on who—or what—does the coding. Large Language Models (LLMs) promise to democratize qualitative analysis, but do high agreement rates translate into equivalent thematic findings? This study compares eight LLMs to human annotators on a multilabel coding task using 3,200 responses from the UC Berkeley Social Networks Study, comprising over 19,000 coding decisions. Although LLM-human reliability does not match human-human reliability overall, LLMs approach human performance on simpler tasks and can serve as useful additional coders for generating consensus labels. Compared to a gold-standard human consensus, models achieve 82–97% per-category agreement, but macro F1 is lower and response-level similarity is lower still: even the best model reproduces the full human label set for fewer than 60% of responses. Yet high agreement masks thematic divergence. Models systematically over-identify themes, assigning 67% more categories per response, especially for categories requiring greater interpretive judgment.

Models also show lower agreement for some demographic groups. These gaps are partly explained by response characteristics such as length, clarity, and atypicality, and some persist after controls, with implications for studies of populations whose response styles diverge from the corpus average. At the sample level, models largely preserve the overall thematic narrative: human and model category rankings correlate strongly (pooled Spearman's ρ=0.75), and top-performing models achieve approximately 80% directional agreement on demographic patterns. Concrete behavioral questions, such as reasons for moving or strategies for making friends, show especially strong alignment. Yet systematic over-classification can still shift narratives about how specific groups behave, leading researchers to report patterns that the human gold standard does not support.

Look out at a forest. What do you see? You see visual masses of green; you see large numbers of leaves; you see the various sizes of the many different trees. Is one of those features more salient than the others? According to a popular view in cognitive science, number is perceptually prioritized over other visuospatial ensemble properties like density and size, such that when you look out at a forest, what you see first and foremost is the number of trees (or trunks, or leaves) rather than their size or their density, etc. The problem with these arguments is that they mostly hinge on comparisons to only one other dimension: cumulative area. Here, we ask a very simple question: Might there be some other dimension that is prioritized over number? Across five unique paradigms and thirteen experiments with over 2,000 participants, we show that human adults prioritize average size over number, such that they are more likely to (a) categorize, (b) explicitly match, (c) notice changes in, and (d) identify extreme instances of that dimension. We additionally show that children behave the same way. For this reason, we argue against the universal salience of number, noting that these ‘competitive’ approaches (i.e., in which dimensions are compared against each other) are often context dependent.

This study examined the relationships among student effort, syllabus coverage, verified mastery, and classroom achievement across four Senior High School mathematics courses at a private Philippine institution during school year 2024-2025. Using data from the McGraw-Hill Assessment and Learning in Knowledge Spaces adaptive platform merged with institutional grade records, 2,584 matched student-subject observations were analyzed across Basic Calculus, General Mathematics, Pre-Calculus, and Statistics and Probability. Pearson correlation analyses revealed significant positive associations between student effort and syllabus coverage across all four subjects, with the strongest relationships observed in General Mathematics and Statistics and Probability. Hierarchical multiple regression established that syllabus coverage contributed significant incremental variance in classroom final grades beyond student effort in all four subjects, with the largest increment in General Mathematics. Effort paradox is when student exertion ceases to be a significant predictor of grades once syllabus coverage is accounted for across all subjects, revealing that time spent on the platform only predicts classroom final grades when it results in measurable curriculum progress. Verified mastery showed stronger alignment with classroom performance in sequentially structured subjects, particularly Pre-Calculus, where prerequisite topic dependency is most explicit. Retention gaps between syllabus coverage and verified mastery were positive across all subjects, with their relationship to classroom performance varying by subject. Findings support a shift in adaptive learning evaluation from time-based engagement indicators toward progress-based and curriculum-aligned metrics, with subject-level differentiation in the role of mastery across the knowledge space.

This study provides experimental evidence for sonority-driven stress in Brazilian Portuguese (BP). We show that speakers systematically prefer final stress when the ultima contains a sonorant coda {N, l, r} rather than the obstruent coda {s}. The effect is specific to the ultima, the position where weight is otherwise most relevant to BP stress. A lexical analysis of monomorphemic words corroborates the experimental pattern: /s/-final words receive final stress less often than sonorant-final words. We further show that this asymmetry cannot be reduced to morphological factors (the plural suffix /-s/ is invisible to stress), nor to a sonority-free account on which final /s/ is a prosodic appendix. These findings bear on a contested question in metrical phonology (whether, and how, segmental sonority conditions stress placement), on which experimental evidence has so far been scarce.

This study examines how affective micropublics emerge in TikTok comment sections during the 2025 German federal election campaign. We conceptualize comment sections as digital micropublics: localized but networked arenas in which users enact publicness through affirmation, opposition, and emotional expression. Empirically, the analysis draws on 12,685 videos from 1,274 political accounts, engagement metrics, and more than two million comments, examined through LLM-based topic classification and automated stance and emotion classification. Methodologically, the study shows how LLM-assisted analysis can move beyond content classification to trace how political messages are taken up, emotionally charged, and redirected in audience interaction. Results show that campaign-related content dominates political TikTok, followed by economic issues, democracy and the political system, social policy, and migration. Yet visibility and audience response vary sharply across parties. The AfD combines high posting frequency with strongly supportive and emotionally aligned comment environments, while centrist and governing parties face predominantly critical or mocking responses. Cross-party hostility analysis further reveals asymmetric patterns of animosity, with negative engagement directed toward specific political opponents rather than distributed randomly. The study shows that TikTok functions simultaneously as a space of participatory visibility and affective polarization. Conceptually, it advances digital micropublics as a framework for analyzing how platformed publics form around political content, emotional alignment, and antagonistic relations.
